title: How Marketplaces Pay Out to Hundreds of Sellers
summary: Learn how marketplace payouts work at scale, from choosing a payout cadence to keeping sub-merchant balances accurate and automating payouts.
body_markdown:
For a marketplace, getting paid is only half the job. The other half is paying out: moving the right amount to every seller, on time, without errors. When a platform has a few dozen sellers, a finance team can handle this by hand. When it has hundreds, payouts become one of the hardest operations in the business.


In a


[Visa and PCMI survey of 2,800 marketplace sellers](https://corporate.visa.com/en/products/visa-direct/blog/transforming-digital-platforms-with-payout-systems.html) across 14 countries, 90% said payout speed is very or extremely important, and 70% said they would consider switching platforms for a better payout experience.


This guide explains how marketplace payouts work at scale, how to choose a payout cadence, and how to keep every seller's balance accurate. In this article, sellers are referred to as sub-merchants, the businesses that receive funds through the marketplace.


Key takeaways


- Marketplace payouts get harder with scale because volume, payout destinations, refunds, and reconciliation all grow at once.


- The right payout cadence balances sub-merchant cash flow against the buffer a platform needs for refunds.


- Accurate per-sub-merchant balances matter as much as payout speed, because they stop over-withdrawals and disputes.


- Automating onboarding, splits, payouts, and reporting in one flow removes most of the manual work.


## Why marketplace payouts get harder as you grow


A single payout looks simple: take what a sub-merchant earned, subtract the platform's commission, and send the rest to their bank account. The difficulty comes from doing that hundreds or thousands of times, every week, with no room for error.


Four things grow at the same time:


- Volume.


More sub-merchants means more transfers, more payout requests, and more support tickets when something is late.


- Destinations.


Sub-merchants bank with different institutions, and some want to be paid to e-wallets instead. Every new destination is another detail to validate before money moves.


- Adjustments.


Refunds, chargebacks, and cancelled orders change what a sub-merchant is owed after the sale. A payout sent too early can leave the platform covering the gap.


- Reconciliation.


Every payout has to match a sale, a commission, and a bank record. When those records live in different systems, the monthly close stretches out.


Access matters too. In the same Visa and PCMI research, 15% of marketplace sellers complained that they could not reach their money outside business hours.


## **How to choose a payout cadence**


Payout cadence is the rhythm at which sub-merchants receive their money. It is a trade-off: faster marketplace payouts help sub-merchants manage cash flow, while slower ones give the platform a buffer for refunds and disputes.


**Cadence**


**How it works** **Best for**


**Trade-off**


On-demand


Sub-merchants withdraw their balance when they choose


Established sub-merchants who manage their own cash


Less predictable outflows for the platform


Daily


Balances are paid out every business day


Food, delivery, and fast-moving goods


Little time to absorb refunds


Weekly


Payouts run on fixed weekdays


Most retail and service marketplaces


Sub-merchants wait longer for cash


Monthly


One payout at the start of each month


High-value or low-frequency sales


Can strain smaller sub-merchants


Many marketplaces combine options, such as a weekly default with on-demand withdrawals for trusted sub-merchants. A holding period can also protect the platform. On Xendit,


[auto-withdrawal](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/auto-withdrawal) runs daily or weekly in Indonesia, with an optional 3- or 7-day balance maturity period. In other markets, it runs daily, weekly, or monthly, with an optional minimum balance.

## **Why accurate balances matter as much as payout speed**


A fast payout is only useful if the amount is right. Many marketplaces track what each sub-merchant is owed in an internal table, then check it against the payment provider's settlement file at month-end. Errors surface weeks after they happen, and a sub-merchant who questions a payout forces the finance team to rebuild the history by hand.


The more reliable approach is a separate ledger for every sub-merchant. Each one has its own balance and transaction history, updated as payments settle, so the platform always knows exactly what can be paid out.


Xendit merchant


[Mekari](https://www.xendit.co/en/case-study/mekari/) shows why this matters. The Indonesian business software company processes payments for thousands of merchants of its own. Before switching, its finance team could not always tell each merchant's exact balance. After moving each merchant to a sub-account with a separate ledger, Mekari's books balanced, and merchants could no longer withdraw more than they had. Its reconciliation team also shrank from five people to two.

## **How to automate marketplace payouts**


Automation works best when the whole flow, from onboarding to reporting, runs through one system. A typical setup has four stages:


1. Onboard and verify sub-merchants.


Each sub-merchant gets its own account and completes business verification before receiving funds.


2. Route payments and take commission.


Incoming payments land in the sub-merchant's balance, and a split rule moves the platform's commission automatically.


3. Pay out on a set schedule or on request.


The platform sends payouts, or sub-merchants withdraw their own balance.


4. Reconcile from one source.


Every payment, split, and payout is recorded against the same account, so reports match without manual cross-checking.

## **Frequently asked questions**


**What are marketplace payouts?**


Marketplace payouts are the transfers a platform sends to its sub-merchants after customers pay. Each payout is the sub-merchant's share of their sales, minus the platform's commission and any fees, refunds, or adjustments.


**How often should a marketplace pay out its sub-merchants?**


There is no single right answer. Daily payouts suit fast-moving categories where sub-merchants need cash quickly, while weekly or monthly payouts give the platform more time to absorb refunds. Many marketplaces set a default schedule and let established sub-merchants withdraw on demand.


**Can sub-merchants choose when to withdraw their money?**


It depends on the platform's setup. On XenPlatform,


[sub-accounts can withdraw from their own dashboards or set their own auto-withdrawal schedules](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/payouts-for-sub-accounts) , while the master account can also create payouts on their behalf.


**What happens if a customer asks for a refund after a payout?**


The platform may need to recover funds from the sub-merchant or cover the refund itself. A holding period reduces this risk. In Indonesia, Xendit's


[auto-withdrawal offers a 3- or 7-day balance maturity period](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/auto-withdrawal) so funds stay available for refunds before they are paid out.


**Do sub-merchants need to be verified before they receive payouts?**


Yes, in most cases. On XenPlatform,


[business verification is mandatory for every sub-account](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/sub-accounts) . The platform can submit documents on the sub-merchant's behalf or invite the sub-merchant to verify directly with Xendit.


**Can a marketplace pay out to e-wallets as well as bank accounts?**


Yes, if the payout provider supports both. Xendit supports


[payouts to bank accounts and e-wallets across Southeast Asia](https://docs.xendit.co/docs) , so platforms can match each sub-merchant's preferred destination.
